title: Corn Flour vs Cornmeal: The Grind Changes More Than the Name

seo.title: Corn Flour vs Cornmeal: What Changes
seo.meta_description: In U.S. cooking, corn flour is finely ground whole corn while cornmeal is coarser. Cornstarch is a separate white starch product, so the three are not interchangeable in every recipe.
seo.search_intent: Clarify U.S. differences among corn flour, cornmeal, and cornstarch, including texture and common uses.

excerpt: In the U.S., corn flour and cornmeal are both ground corn, but corn flour is much finer. Cornstarch is different again: it is isolated starch used mainly for thickening rather than for the grain texture of cornbread or polenta.
content_html:
A recipe that says corn flour can be confusing because the term changes across countries. In U.S. cooking, corn flour usually means very finely ground corn, cornmeal is coarser, and cornstarch is the isolated white starch. They come from the same crop but do not behave the same way.

Grind size changes the eating texture

Corn flour is milled finely enough to feel powdery and produces a smoother batter or dough. Cornmeal retains larger particles, so cooked dishes keep more grainy texture. Fine, medium, and coarse cornmeal can all give noticeably different results.

Processing matters too. Masa harina is nixtamalized corn flour, while precooked corn flours used for arepas have been cooked and dried before milling. They hydrate differently from plain corn flour.

Cornstarch is not a finer version of cornmeal

Cornstarch is made by separating the starch fraction from the kernel. It is nearly white, has little corn flavor, and swells strongly in hot liquid. That makes it useful for gravy, pudding, and stir-fry sauce, but it cannot provide the grain structure of polenta or cornbread.

IngredientWhat it isCommon use
Corn flourFinely ground cornBatters, breads, dusting, blending into dough
CornmealCoarser ground cornPolenta, grits-style dishes, cornbread
CornstarchIsolated corn starchThickening sauces and fillings

Country matters when reading a recipe

British recipes often use cornflour to mean what Americans call cornstarch. If a U.K. custard recipe asks for cornflour, do not reach for a bag of U.S. whole-grain corn flour. Check the recipe's origin and the described function.

For U.S. recipes, think fine grain, coarse grain, isolated starch: corn flour, cornmeal, cornstarch.

faq.question: Is corn flour the same as cornmeal?
faq.answer: In U.S. terminology they are both ground corn, but corn flour is finer and cornmeal is coarser, so texture changes.

faq.question: Is corn flour the same as cornstarch?
faq.answer: Not in the U.S. Cornstarch is isolated starch; corn flour is finely ground corn.

faq.question: Why do British recipes call cornstarch cornflour?
faq.answer: The vocabulary differs by region. In the U.K., cornflour usually means the white starch Americans call cornstarch.
